variants.hypothesis: Performance: cache each settled Markdown block's element tree by its text in a 500-entry LRU, so rows that scroll back into the virtualised list do not parse their Markdown again.
Hierarchy: a hairline rule at the start of every turn but the first, as T3 Code rules off a settled turn's work, so turn boundaries scan in a long session.

verdicts.reasons: The only visible difference is how turns are separated: A draws a full-width hairline rule before each new user message (default, streaming, mobile, and between every step in long-content), while B leaves a clear gap and lets the right-aligned user bubble mark the new turn. B is closer to T3 Code, where turns are split by space and the only rules are the faint 'Worked for' header line and the changed-files card, so B gets the higher fidelity and cost scores; in long-content A's rule repeats 300 times without adding anything the bubble does not already show. A's rule does make turn edges a little easier to spot when scrolling, so hierarchy is a tie, and the gap in B is not loose enough to cost it density. Everything else is the same in both: the with-cards story (amber vault and browser cards, indigo question card, matching the vault reference), the three-dot streaming placeholder, the spinner on 'Running pnpm test', and the wrapped long link. Both share the same weaknesses: in default and with-cards the screenshot starts mid-scroll, cutting off the 'Worked for' row and the top of the vault card, and at 420px the code block is cut off at 'idempoter' with no sign that it scrolls.

The with-cards story is the same in both, and so is all the copy. Everywhere else the only visible difference is how turns are separated. B draws a full-width hairline above each user message (default, streaming, long-content and mobile-420), while A uses only vertical space. In long-content, B's lines make each tenant step a little easier to pick out, but the right-aligned user bubble already marks where a turn starts, so the line repeats that cue in every turn. T3 Code's transcript separates turns with space and keeps rules for structural rows like 'Worked for 3m 43s', so A reads closer to it and is more restrained. Spacing scale, type, cards, status colours, the streaming dots and the 420px layout are otherwise identical, including the content clipped at the top of the scroll area in both, so the other scores are the same.

Every story is the same in A and B except for how turns are separated: A draws a full-width hairline above each new user message, and B uses only extra vertical space. In long-content, the right-aligned user bubble and the gap already mark where each turn starts, so A's lines between Step 298/299/300 repeat that signal and add horizontal stripes. That is the only thing pulling A down on cost. B's space-only rhythm is closer to T3 Code's transcript, where 'Worked for 3m 43s' blocks and user bubbles are set apart mostly by space, so B reads a little calmer and closer to the fidelity reference. Both share the same weaknesses, which keep them from top marks: in default and mobile-420 the top of the transcript is cut off mid-line at the frame edge, the code block runs off the side at 420px, and long-content says '1 duplicate invoices'. with-cards and streaming look identical in both, and the cards match the Harbour vault card's amber border, radius and status colours.

variants.hypothesis: Fidelity: while a turn works, the transcript ends with T3 Code's working row, 'Working for 12s' timed from the turn's start, instead of three animated dots, so the live duration the tool rows gave up is told at turn level.

verdicts.reasons: A and B look the same in default, long-content, with-cards and mobile-420: same quiet 'Worked for 50s, 4 steps' summaries, user bubbles, code block, tool rows with the sky spinner, and the same cards. The only visible difference is the streaming story before the first word arrives. A shows a muted 'Working for 30s' line under the user message. That matches T3's 'Worked for 3m 43s' row and Harbour's session list, which pairs 'Working' with an elapsed time ('3m 20s'). B shows three grey typing dots instead, a generic chat pattern that says nothing about how long the agent has been working and appears nowhere else in Harbour. That costs B on states, fidelity, consistency, copy and cost, at both 1280 and 420. A shared weakness at 420 is that the code block is cut off at 'idempoter' with no visible way to scroll, so mobile scores the same for both.

Default, long-content and with-cards look the same in A and B at both widths, and mobile-420 shows no visible difference, so those criteria start equal. The difference is in the streaming story before the answer arrives. A shows a quiet muted row, 'Working for 30s', under the user's message. That matches T3's 'Worked for 3m 43s' and the elapsed time Harbour's session list shows next to Working (3m 20s), and it pairs well with A's own 'Worked for 50s, 4 steps' summary above. B shows only three grey dots there, a generic typing indicator that hides how long the agent has been working. The dots also look unlike anything else in Harbour or T3, and the same loss shows in streaming-420. Both share the same weaknesses: the default story is clipped at the top, cutting off 'Thought it through', and at 420px the code block is cut off at 'idempoter' with no sign that it scrolls.

The streaming story is the only place A and B really differ; the default, long-content, with-cards and mobile shots look the same in both. Before the answer arrives, A shows a muted 'Working for 30s' line at 1280 and 420. That matches T3's 'Worked for 3m 43s' header, the 'Worked for 50s, 4 steps' rows above it, and the elapsed time Harbour's session list shows. B shows three grey dots there instead. That is a generic chat typing indicator that says nothing about how long the agent has been working. It also doesn't match the text-led look of the rest of the transcript. Both versions share the same weaknesses elsewhere: the default story is scrolled so 'Thought it through' is cut off at the top of the frame, and the long code line is cropped at 420. Because the stories are otherwise identical, A wins only on states, fidelity, consistency, copy, cost and mobile.
